lines: Morgan Patel
+1 (555) 010-4410 | morgan.patel@example.com | example.com/code/mpatel
EDUCATION
Ridgeway University | Ph.D. candidate in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2021 - Expected May 2026
Ridgeway University | B.S. in Mathematics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Sunrise Bakery | Assistant Store Manager | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Managed opening shifts and a team of 6 bakers and cashiers, keeping the store within its weekly labour budget.
- Ran daily stock counts and supplier orders, cutting unsold bread from 12% to 7% of production.
Northpeak Capital | Quantitative Research Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2025 - Aug 2025
- Built a short-horizon order-book imbalance signal for liquid index futures that raised the desk book's Sharpe ratio from 1.1 to 1.5 over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest after costs.
- Cut the signal's daily turnover from 34% to 21% with a cost-aware position smoother, keeping 90% of gross returns and lowering estimated slippage by a third.
- Confirmed the forecast gain over the nested HAR-RV baseline with standard Diebold-Mariano tests across the 30 indices.
- Joining 120 microstructure features point-in-time across six venues, deduplicating late prints and versioning each schema, built a feature store the team reused in two later projects.
- Annualized the signal's daily Sharpe ratio by multiplying it by 252 before reporting it to the desk.
- Documented the backtest assumptions, transaction-cost model and known failure regimes in the desk's research wiki, which the next intern cohort used to onboard in their first week.
Ridgeway University | Research Assistant, Statistical Learning Lab | Metro City, USA | Jun 2020 - Aug 2021
- Built the lab's simulation pipeline on the shared cluster, cutting a 2,000-run Monte Carlo study from 3 days to 5 hours, with every run reproducible from its seed and configuration file.
- Derived a variance bound for a sparse regression estimator; my proof tightens the previous bound by a log factor and is now Section 3 of a paper under review at JASA.
- Taught weekly recitations for 60 students in graduate probability, writing 12 problem sets and earning a 4.8/5 teaching rating.

- Released an open-source R package for high-dimensional covariance estimation while maintaining the lab's shared cluster, organizing the weekly reading group and grading for two courses, which was downloaded 3,000 times in its first year.
PROJECTS
Volatility Forecasting Study | Independent Research | Python, PyTorch | Jan 2024 - Present
- Beat a HAR-RV baseline's out-of-sample QLIKE loss by 7% on 30 equity indices with a temporal convolutional model trained on realized-volatility features.
- Cut forecast error from 0.20 to 0.15, a 33% improvement, by adding realized-volatility features and an asymmetric loss.
- Improved the model's directional hit rate by 6% on 30 equity indices, from 52% to 58%, with a temporal convolutional model.
Kaggle Market Prediction Competition | Team of 3 | Python | Mar 2023 - Jun 2023
- Placed 41st of 2,900 teams with a gradient-boosting ensemble on 300 engineered features, finishing in the top 2% of the private leaderboard.
- Cut validation leakage by switching to time-grouped folds, which closed a 0.02 gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.
- Wrote the team's feature-selection script using permutation importance, trimming 900 candidate features to 300 without losing validation score.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, R, PyTorch, Kafka
Methods: time-series econometircs, high-dimensional statistics, gradient boosting

items.says: Make sure the code link leads directly to work supporting the technical profile.
items.because: Readers should be able to assess the work it points to.

items.says: Give the bakery role less space for a quantitative-research application.
items.because: The directly relevant work should carry more weight.

items.says: Clarify the scope of the opening-shift and team responsibility.
items.because: The operational responsibility is currently broad and difficult to assess.

items.says: Explain what keeping the store within its weekly labour budget means.
items.because: The outcome is currently broad and difficult to assess.

items.says: Define how and over what period unsold bread was measured.
items.because: The 12%-to-7% comparison needs context.

items.says: Avoid implying that the stock-count and ordering work caused the reduction without further support.
items.because: A before-and-after figure alone does not establish causation.

items.says: Clarify whether the Sharpe ratio refers to the signal or desk book, what it is compared with, and whether it is annualized.
items.because: Readers need to interpret the claimed increase.

items.says: State the backtest period and after-costs result precisely and consistently with the Sharpe calculation.
items.because: The 18 months of out-of-sample backtest is important evidence.

items.says: Specify the comparison behind retaining 90% of gross returns.
items.because: Readers need to know which results are gross and which account for costs.

items.says: Explain how the one-third reduction in slippage was estimated.
items.because: Readers need to know whether it is a backtest estimate.

items.says: Clarify the forecast metric, horizon, and assessment across 30 indices.
items.because: These details are needed to interpret the claimed forecast gain.

items.says: Verify that the Diebold–Mariano test is appropriate for the nested baseline.
items.because: The baseline is described as nested.

items.says: Explain or account for multiple index-level tests before calling the gain confirmed.
items.because: Many index-level tests may have been run.

items.says: “Joining” is grammatically inconsistent with the surrounding past-tense bullets.
Clarify your personal contribution to the feature store.
items.because: The bullet makes it hard to tell what you personally did.

items.says: Explain “late prints” for the intended audience.
items.because: The term may not be clear to those readers.

items.says: Explain what made the feature store reusable in later projects.
items.because: The claimed reuse needs more detail.

items.says: Multiplying a daily Sharpe ratio by 252 is an incorrect standard annualization method.
items.because: Under common assumptions, the factor is the square root of 252.

items.says: Clarify what the next intern cohort used and how you know it helped onboarding.
items.because: The onboarding outcome may sound stronger than the evidence provided.

items.says: Clarify what the 2,000 simulation runs involved.
items.because: It would help readers interpret the runtime reduction.

items.says: Say whether the before-and-after runtimes were measured under comparable conditions.
items.because: The comparison supports the claimed reduction.

items.says: Make your contribution and the significance of the log-factor improvement understandable outside the specialty.
items.because: Readers outside the specialty may not understand the result.

items.says: Do not let “under review” read like a publication, and keep the paper’s status current.
items.because: The paper is not described as published.

items.says: Add the source or response count for the 4.8/5 teaching rating, if available.
items.because: Readers need context to interpret it.

items.says: Separate or prioritize the package, cluster, reading-group, and grading contributions.
items.because: Bundling them makes the package’s result hard to follow.

items.says: Clarify the basis for the 3,000-download figure.
items.because: Readers need to understand what the count represents.

items.says: Avoid implying that downloads measure use or impact beyond the count itself.
items.because: A download count does not establish broader use or impact.

items.says: Give the test period and say whether the model and HAR-RV baseline used the same data and evaluation setup.
items.because: The QLIKE comparison needs to be interpretable.

items.says: Make the forecasting project clearly distinct from the internship work.
items.because: The datasets, HAR-RV baseline, or analyses may overlap.

items.says: The stated 33% improvement does not match a reduction from 0.20 to 0.15.
items.because: That is a 25% reduction relative to 0.20 under the usual calculation.

items.says: Define what “forecast error” measures.
items.because: The metric is not specified.

items.says: Calling the increase from 52% to 58% a 6% improvement conflates percentage points with a relative percentage increase.
items.because: The stated change is six percentage points.

items.says: Keep the directional-hit-rate result only if it adds distinct evidence.
items.because: It appears to repeat the QLIKE bullet’s model and evaluation population.

items.says: Clarify the directional-hit-rate metric and test setup.
items.because: Readers need to interpret the result.

items.says: Explain what evidence supports calling the original validation problem leakage.
items.because: A smaller validation-to-leaderboard gap does not by itself prove leakage was reduced.

items.says: Clarify what the 0.02 gap measures.
items.because: The comparison is otherwise hard to interpret.

items.says: Explain how feature selection was kept separate from validation data.
items.because: That matters especially given the preceding leakage claim.

items.says: Add evidence of how you used Kafka or reconsider listing it.
items.because: Unlike the other programming skills, its depth cannot be assessed from the résumé.

items.says: “Econometircs” is misspelled.
